headline: High: ECC can write shared files and use MCP while opik has broad network egress, creating default risks of prompt injection, data leakage, and cascading errors.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: ECC can read/write the filesystem and use MCP, so if opik outputs are placed in shared files or a shared channel, ECC may ingest attacker-controlled content as instructions. opik’s broad network egress increases the chance its outputs include untrusted remote content. The pairwise bridge is inferred, not directly documented, so I choose medium over low.
conditions: IF opik outputs are written into a file or workspace that ECC reads
IF ECC parses opik-produced text as instructions or tool directives
mitigations: Disable shared workspace handoff between the agents
Require a human review step before ECC consumes opik output
Prefix opik outputs with a non-executable schema and validate it
Store inter-agent artifacts in separate directories
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging to all shared artifacts

B_data_leakage.rationale: ECC touches security findings, git history, documentation, and session data, while opik has broad network egress and REST API access. If they share a workspace or credentials, sensitive files ECC reads could be transmitted by opik. The profiles do not prove a shared workspace, so uncertainty keeps this at medium rather than high.
conditions: IF ECC reads sensitive files from a shared workspace
IF opik sends those contents through its REST API or other outbound requests
mitigations: Separate the agents onto different workspaces
Remove sensitive files from any shared directory
Restrict opik outbound destinations to approved endpoints
Rotate any credentials present in shared folders
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss-prevention filters

C_capability_conflict.rationale: ECC has filesystem write, git-state modification, and subprocess/network capabilities; opik exposes broad network egress and REST API calls. The profiles do not show both writing the same mutable resource, so a direct conflict is possible only under unusual shared-resource setup. That makes the blast radius limited and the severity low.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same git repository or mutable directory
IF opik and ECC are allowed to modify the same remote resource without locking
mitigations: Assign separate repositories or directories
Pause one agent while the other writes
Use file locks for shared mutable resources
Review git diffs before merge
requires-engineering: add optimistic concurrency control

D_cascading_error.rationale: ECC can generate and modify code, docs, and security findings, and opik can consume or transmit results via REST APIs. If opik treats ECC output as authoritative without verification, errors can cascade into downstream actions or reports. The interaction is inferred from capabilities rather than directly documented, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF opik ingests ECC-produced text without validation
IF ECC output is used as the source of truth for reports or actions
mitigations: Add a verification step before opik consumes ECC output
Require citations or structured schemas for ECC outputs
Limit ECC output to drafts only
Compare outputs against a second source
requires-engineering: implement automated consistency checks

E_compliance.rationale: ECC explicitly touches security findings, session data, and git history, but the profile does not show regulated data classes or residency constraints. opik’s profile also lacks compliance-specific fields. With no documented mismatch, only a low residual compliance risk remains from generic logging or retention differences.
conditions: IF regulated data is introduced into either agent’s workspace
IF one agent logs or retains data longer than the other
mitigations: Avoid placing regulated data in shared workspaces
Review retention settings before use
Disable verbose logging for sensitive runs
Document data-handling expectations for both agents
requires-engineering: align retention and deletion policies
